transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-30 15:00 PST | Duration: 58m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Rao (CTO, Cobalt), Marcus (Platform Eng), Sara (ML Eng)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro — Maya from Redwood, Liam is our solutions engineer. Priya, Marcus, Sara, thanks for joining.
[00:14] Priya (Cobalt): Thanks — short on time today so we want to focus on acceptance criteria for a pilot and what you need from us.
[00:23] Liam (Redwood SE): Great. The core ask we heard was to validate latency targets and cost under your traffic mix, right? And to recommend whether first-token TTFT or per-token TPOT should drive the SLOs.
[00:34] Marcus (Cobalt): Yeah, correct. Our primary product is a clinical summarization API used in the EHR flow. User-facing UX wants the first sentence fast but also overall generation cost matters.
[00:46] Sara (Cobalt): And we have... um, a fairly spiky pattern around chart closing, so bursts of traffic at shift change.
[00:54] Maya: Perfect. Quick clarification on terms so we're aligned — when I say TTFT, I mean time-to-first-token measured from request arrival to first token emitted; TPOT we're using per-token average or p95 per-token latency aggregated across full responses. We typically measure TTFT at p95 and p99 and TPOT as p95 per-token and p99 across token steps, plus aggregate per-request total token time.
[01:19] Priya: Okay, we need both because physicians care about the first sentence being visible quickly, but billing is per-token so we need per-token efficiency.
[01:28] Liam: Right. For the pilot we usually define acceptance as: TTFT p95 <= 400ms and p99 <= 900ms for the short prompt path (<= 128 tokens output). For longer generation (>= 512 tokens) we look at TPOT p95 <= 25ms/token and p99 <= 60ms/token as a target. These numbers are examples — we should tune to your UX.
[01:51] Marcus: Those targets seem aggressive — are they on dedicated infra or hosted?
[01:55] Liam: Good question. That depends on the model/backends. On Redwood Dedicated with pinned GPU pools we see closer to those numbers for mid-sized models (7B-13B) with quantization. Hosted endpoints on shared capacity can meet TTFT targets for many workloads but TPOT can vary under bursty load. We'll include both dedicated and hosted candidate runs in the benchmark.
[02:17] Sara: How do you instrument measurement? We need to be able to reproduce in our test environment.
[02:21] Liam: We provide a measurement harness: traffic generator (replays and synthetic mixture), an agent that records request timestamps client-side and server-side, and scripts to compute TTFT and TPOT percentiles. We'll deliver a jenkins/github action style script you can run. We'll also capture token-level timing via streaming events. Note: sometimes streaming timestamps get noisy if network jitter is high, so we capture both server-side and client-side.
[02:46] Priya: On data: our traces have PHI. We need to know about data residency and KMS, encryption at rest.
[02:52] Maya: Understood. We'll send our security summary: SOC2/ISO mapping, KMS integration options, private VPC deployment details. For the pilot we can run on Private (VPC) or Dedicated depending on contract. We'll include redaction and audit log guidance.
[03:08] Marcus: Good. Also wondering about warmup — do you recommend pre-warming to stabilize KV cache?
[03:13] Liam: Yes, warmup matters. For chat-style workloads we prime the KV cache and preload common system prompts. We'll include a warmup stage in the benchmark plan — like 15 minutes of ramp plus a 30-minute steady state run to collect p95/p99.
[03:26] Priya: Walk us through acceptance criteria proposals.
[03:29] Liam: Proposal A (UX-first): TTFT p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 800ms for short responses; TPOT p95 <= 30ms/token for long responses. Proposal B (cost-first): TTFT p95 <= 600ms, p99 <= 1.2s but target TPOT average < 40ms/token to keep cost down. Proposal C (hybrid): TTFT p95 <= 450ms, p99 <= 900ms and TPOT p95 <= 35ms/token, plus 99th percentile end-to-end request success > 99.5%.
[03:58] Priya: I like hybrid, but we need quantifiable pass/fail for the POC.
[04:03] Maya: So how about acceptance: hybrid thresholds, and two additional gating checks — cost per 1k tokens delta vs your current baseline < 15%, and functional fidelity regression < 2% on a reference eval set?
[04:17] Sara: What do you mean by fidelity regression?
[04:19] Liam: We run a curated prompt set and compute automated metrics (like ROUGE/BLEU where applicable) plus a small human spot-check. If output quality drops more than 2% against your baseline model then it's a fail.
[04:33] Marcus: Baseline is currently our in-house tuned 13B model running on our infra — cost numbers are pretty high, but we're working on quantization.
[04:41] Priya: Timeline — we can get traces by end of week, but infra signoff might take longer. We want to run the pilot in the next three weeks ideally.
[04:50] Maya: That timeline is feasible. Our recommended schedule: week 1 share traces & prompts; week 2 benchmark setup & warmup; week 3 2-day pilot runs and analysis.
[04:59] Priya: Sounds good.
[05:03] Liam: About workload sizing — can you share typical QPS and token distribution?
[05:07] Marcus: Average qps is 8 with peaks to ~70 during shift changes, median response token length is 80 tokens, 90th perc around 420 tokens.
[05:17] Liam: Helpful. For benchmark we'll create a traffic mix with three buckets: short (<= 128 tokens) 55% traffic, medium (129-512) 30%, long (>512) 15%; a burst pattern with 1-minute spikes to 8x baseline to emulate shift change.
[05:34] Sara: And concurrency? Our app holds connections open — average concurrency around 40, spikes to 300.
[05:41] Liam: We'll put concurrency targets into the harness — and test both steady and burst load. For server-side metrics we'll capture GPU utilization, queue lengths, batch sizes, and p99 queue wait.
[05:53] Priya: On metrics collection — we need logs for audit and per-token breakdowns for billing. Can you expose per-request token counts and timings?
[05:59] Maya: Yes, per-request telemetry is available in Redwood Console (or via logs in Private). We'll include token histograms per minute and exportable CSVs.
[06:08] Marcus: Any known gotchas when measuring TTFT? We've seen noise when clients use reverse proxies.
[06:13] Liam: Proxy time can bias client-side TTFT — that's why we capture server side emit timestamps too. Also note that models with dynamic compilation (jit) can have long cold first-token times; we'll account for that by ensuring the model is JIT compiled and warmed before measurement.
[06:28] Priya: For the SLO windows, are you suggesting rolling windows or calendar windows for p95/p99?
[06:34] Liam: For pilot acceptance we recommend a steady-state 30-minute rolling window to compute p95/p99, and also report 24-hour aggregates for visibility. For long-term SLOs, rolling windows typically drive alerts.
[06:47] Sara: How do you separate tokenization differences between models? Token counts vary and affect TPOT.
[06:51] Liam: We'll normalize by using your tokenization pipeline in the harness. We'll also report per-model effective tokens and convert to cost-normalized metrics.
[06:59] Priya: Any fallback strategy if the dedicated capacity hits latency regressions?
[07:03] Maya: Redwood supports policy-based fallback — e.g., route to a smaller but lower-latency model for TTFT-critical paths, or throttle non-critical requests during spikes. We'll propose a routing policy as part of the POC playbook.
[07:17] Marcus: Regarding security again — if we use Private VPC do you need to pull any logs out?
[07:22] Maya: In Private deployments we can keep logs within your VPC. Audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM via secure endpoints. KMS integration for keys is supported. We'll attach the security integration matrix.
[07:35] Priya: Good. Let's talk pass/fail criteria for the benchmark run itself.
[07:39] Liam: We'll do a two-run approach: run A - hosted candidate models, run B - dedicated backends. Each run has warmup then two 30-minute steady state windows. Pass criteria: both TTFT and TPOT hybrid thresholds met in at least one run, quality regression < 2%, and cost delta within agreed bounds. If neither run meets thresholds, we'll produce a remediation plan with tuning suggestions (batching, quantization, KV cache tweaks).
[08:08] Sara: On quantization, do you support int8-rounding and awareness of kernel selection?
[08:12] Liam: Yes, our runtime supports several quantization profiles; we'll test a conservative int8-like profile and a faster lower-precision profile. We'll log memory use and error metrics per profile.
[08:22] Marcus: How long to set up the dedicated pool if we choose that path?
[08:25] Maya: For Dedicated it's typically 2-3 business days after contract and capacity reservation, but for pilot we can often use a temporary reservation to expedite.
[08:34] Priya: Do you have an example benchmark doc?
[08:36] Maya: Yes — I'll share a benchmark charter doc. (Link: https://redwood.example.com/pilot-charter/cobalt-2026) Please note link is shorthand; full doc attached in follow-up email.
[08:47] Marcus: Cool. For the measurement script, do you produce the percentiles or do we run analytics?
[08:51] Liam: The harness outputs pre-computed percentiles and raw event logs. We can also send you a summary CSV and a notebook with plots.
[08:58] Priya: Any recommended sampling for long runs to reduce cost?
[09:02] Liam: We recommend sampling 10% of long responses for token-level timing but keep full capture for TTFT and request-level metrics. That keeps data volumes reasonable.
[09:13] Sara: What about functional tests — do you support evaluating hallucination or label-run fidelity?
[09:17] Liam: We provide an evaluation harness; for hallucination detection we can run a set of closed-answer prompts and compute exact-match/answer consistency. We'll also support a small human annotation pass if you want.
[09:31] Priya: Ok then. On acceptance threshold — can we tie SLO to business KPIs? e.g., physician triage completion rate within 2 minutes?
[09:40] Maya: Absolutely — we can map TTFT and TPOT to downstream KPIs and include that in the acceptance matrix. We'll need trace correlation data to do that mapping.
[09:50] Marcus: Are there any license or usage locks with using your curated open models?
[09:54] Maya: We include a catalog of community models plus Redwood-verified variants. Licensing is model dependent; we'll list license terms in the catalog and highlight any restricts.
[10:03] Priya: Great. So immediate actions: we will share traces and prompts, you will send the benchmark charter and security docs, and Liam will prepare the harness.
[10:12] Maya: Exactly. Anything else?
[10:15] Sara: One more question — in your measurement, do you capture cold-start outliers separately?
[10:19] Liam: Yes — we exclude first-cold JIT compile requests from acceptance windows and report them separately. But we also measure cold-start tail for operations.
[10:29] Priya: Ok that addresses my main concerns.
[10:32] Maya: I'll summarize next steps in email after the call. Thanks everyone.
[10:37] Priya: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:40] [Call ends early — the team stayed on for a quick 10-min follow up off-record about billing model]

Notes/summary: Hybrid SLO preferred; pilot acceptance requires meeting hybrid latency thresholds + cost delta bounds + quality regression guardrails. Benchmark plan: traffic mix (short/med/long), burst pattern, warmup, steady-state windows, dedicated + hosted runs, per-token sampling. Security items: SOC2/ISO, VPC/KMS integration, audit logs. Shared artifacts: pilot charter link (see above), security whitepaper forthcoming, traffic traces to be uploaded to shared S3.
